clinicalPearls: X-linked dominant disorder caused by variants in IKBKG (NEMO); usually lethal in males in utero, so it predominantly affects females
Skin lesions evolve through four classic stages along Blaschko lines: vesicular, verrucous, hyperpigmented (whorled/swirled), and atrophic/hypopigmented
The blistering first stage in a neonate can be mistaken for infection, and there is often a peripheral eosinophilia
Associated dental anomalies (peg or missing teeth), alopecia, and nail dystrophy are common
Ocular involvement includes a retinal vasculopathy that can cause retinal detachment and blindness if not detected
Neurological complications (seizures, stroke-like episodes, developmental delay) may occur, mainly in the neonatal period
Diagnosis rests on characteristic staged skin findings, Blaschkoid distribution, and IKBKG genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Incontinentia pigmenti is caused by loss-of-function variants in IKBKG, encoding NEMO, an essential regulatory component of the NF-kappaB signalling pathway. NF-kappaB activation protects cells from apoptosis and coordinates inflammatory responses, so cells that carry the mutation on the active X chromosome are prone to death and to abnormal inflammatory signalling. Random X-inactivation produces a mosaic of affected and unaffected cells, explaining the Blaschko-linear pattern of skin lesions and the variable multisystem involvement. The histological hallmark of 'pigment incontinence', with melanin dropping from damaged basal keratinocytes into the dermis, gives the disorder its name.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal herpes simplex or bullous impetigo (vesicular stage)
Epidermolytic ichthyosis and other blistering genodermatoses
additionalInvestigations: IKBKG molecular genetic testing (including the common deletion)
Skin biopsy showing stage-dependent features including eosinophilic spongiosis or dermal pigment incontinence
Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia in the neonatal period
Urgent paediatric ophthalmology review with retinal examination and fluorescein angiography
Neuroimaging and EEG if neurological symptoms occur
redFlags: Retinal neovascularisation or detachment threatening vision
Neonatal seizures or stroke-like neurological events
Extensive vesicular eruption mistaken for, or complicated by, infection
reference.prognosis: The skin manifestations are generally self-limiting and evolve to subtle residual changes, and most affected females have a normal lifespan; overall prognosis is determined largely by the presence and severity of ocular and neurological involvement.
pitfalls: Mistaking the neonatal vesicular stage for herpes or bacterial infection and delaying diagnosis
Failing to arrange prompt retinal screening, risking preventable visual loss
Overlooking the diagnostic significance of Blaschko-linear lesions and eosinophilia
Not counselling about X-linked inheritance and male lethality for family planning
